passage:
I’m Akash, Arnab’s roommate. On Thursday he packed a water bottle, his ID card and a phone charger before breakfast. The campus march about hostel fees had been approved by the college office, and volunteers had a plan.
Arnab was very quiet. He called home, said only that he had exams next week, and hung up. His hands trembled as he tied his shoes.
He came back at dusk with a sunburnt face and a paper badge. “Everyone stayed calm,” he said. “I was scared at the start. Then a stranger shared her water.” I don’t know what he felt, exactly, but he was smiling.

qa.q: What did Arnab pack before the march?
qa.a: Arnab packed a water bottle, his ID card and a phone charger.

qa.q: What might Arnab have been feeling as his hands trembled?
qa.a: He was probably afraid, and also determined to go. His quiet manner and shaking hands showed fear, but he went anyway.

qa.q: What choices in the passage kept the march safer?
qa.a: The march had been approved by the college office, volunteers had a plan, and Arnab carried water, ID and a charger. Everyone stayed calm.

qa.q: How might the stranger who shared water have felt?
qa.a: The stranger may have wanted to make a scared newcomer feel welcome. Sharing water was a small, warm sign of solidarity.

grounding: Shows a young adult joining a peaceful, approved march with fear, pride and solidarity together, seen by a roommate.

passage:
Monday. Madhuri sat with her notes for the term exam and a message from the lake-protection group. A permit had been granted for a peaceful walk on Friday. Her friend Sudha said, “I’m going. Come with me?” Madhuri’s stomach twisted.
Thursday. She told her parents about it. They worried aloud, and she promised to stay near the organisers and leave if things turned tense.
Friday. The crowd was bigger than she expected. Her heart pounded, but organisers with armbands walked along the line and reminded people to stay calm. A stranger smiled and passed her a water bottle.
Saturday, she was back at her desk, tired and glad.

qa.q: What kind of event was Madhuri considering on Friday?
qa.a: It was a peaceful walk for the lake-protection group, and a permit had been granted.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling at the start of the walk?
qa.a: Madhuri was scared, with her heart pounding, and also proud to be there. The organisers' reminders and the stranger's kindness helped steady her.

qa.q: What choices did Madhuri make to balance the cause against the risks?
qa.a: She told her parents, promised to stay near the organisers and to leave if it turned tense. She also went with a friend to a permitted event.

qa.q: How might Sudha have felt when Madhuri said yes?
qa.a: Sudha was probably glad and reassured to have company. Sudha had invited Madhuri directly, so it mattered to her.

grounding: Shows a young adult weighing risk against a cause and joining a peaceful protest with fear, pride and solidarity.

passage:
'You're coming, right?' Swati tied a strip of white cloth round her wrist. 'Everyone's meeting at the main gate at four.'
Harish sat on his bed, holding his phone. 'My exam's tomorrow. And Papa said if I get into trouble, he'll—'
'It's a peaceful march. Candles, posters, that's it. The fee hike hits you more than me.'
'I know.' He looked at the poster on the desk: FAIR FEES FOR ALL. His heart was thumping. 'What if the police stop it?'
'Then we stand quietly and go home. The union has permission, and the route's on every flyer.'
'...Okay. One hour. Then I'm studying.'
At the gate, three hundred students stood holding candles in silence. Harish's hands shook, and then someone started singing the college song, and he sang too, loudly. Swati squeezed his arm.

qa.q: What did the poster say?
qa.a: FAIR FEES FOR ALL.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling at the gate?
qa.a: Nervous, with shaking hands, and then proud and part of something when he sang with everyone.

qa.q: How did Harish weigh the risks before going?
qa.a: He thought about his exam and his father, checked that the march was peaceful and permitted, and limited himself to one hour.

qa.q: What was it like for Swati to have Harish join?
qa.a: She seemed glad and supportive, squeezing his arm, since the fee hike hit him hardest.

grounding: A student joins a peaceful protest, feeling fear, pride and solidarity, after weighing exams and family worries.

passage: I'd never been to a protest before that night. After a student was harassed near the campus bus stop and the administration did nothing for two weeks, my friend Chandrika said, 'I'm going. You?' My stomach knotted. My parents were in Nagpur and would panic if they saw me on the news. I had lab reports due. But I also thought about walking to that bus stop alone every evening. So I texted Amma where I'd be, and went. Five hundred of us walked from the library to the admin block, holding up phone torches, completely silent. I was scared the whole time, and proud, and part of something enormous. The next week the college put up lights and a guard at the bus stop. I'm Charu. I still get goosebumps.

qa.q: How many students walked from the library to the admin block?
qa.a: Five hundred.

qa.q: How did Charu feel during the march?
qa.a: Scared the whole time, but also proud and part of something enormous.

qa.q: What did Charu do to reduce the risk before going?
qa.a: Texted Amma the plan and joined a silent, peaceful march with a friend.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt when Charu came along?
qa.a: Probably relieved and encouraged, glad not to go alone.

grounding: A young adult joins a peaceful campus march out of conviction, feeling fear, pride and solidarity together.

passage: Faculty mentor's note, Thursday. Sharmila, from my second-year group, came to see me before today's march for the farm workers' wage campaign. She wanted to go but was scared: her scholarship depends on attendance, and her uncle had warned her about 'getting a record'. We talked it through. I told her the march had police permission and a fixed route, and that attendance would be excused for registered participants. She decided to go for two hours with her friend Santosh, stay near the front marshals and leave before dark. She came back at six, sunburnt and shaking a little. 'I was terrified, and I've never felt so proud,' she said. I have asked the department to share the excused-attendance rule with all students.

qa.q: Why was Sharmila worried about her scholarship?
qa.a: It depends on attendance.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel after the march?
qa.a: Terrified and also prouder than ever, sunburnt and a little shaky.

qa.q: How did Sharmila weigh the risk before joining?
qa.a: She talked with her mentor, checked the march had permission and excused attendance, and planned to go with Santosh for two hours near the marshals and leave before dark.

qa.q: What might Santosh's company have meant to Sharmila?
qa.a: Having a friend beside her likely made her feel safer and less alone during the march.

grounding: A mentor's note on a student who weighs risks to studies and family before joining a peaceful march, and feels fear and pride.

passage:
Thursday, late.
Went to the march today. Nearly didn't. At 9 a.m. I was still in the hostel, telling myself I had a lab record due and Papa would be furious if my name came up anywhere. Then Usha texted: "We're at the gate. Your choice, no pressure." That "no pressure" did it. There were maybe three hundred of us, walking from the gate to the admin block about the library closing at six. Police stood at the corner, and my heart hammered every time one of them looked our way. Usha held one end of the banner; I held the other. When we all sang outside the admin block, my throat went tight in a good way. Nobody threw anything. We left at one, as planned. Lab record still due. Haven't told Papa yet. I will, calmly, on Sunday.
Tushar

qa.q: What was the march about?
qa.a: About the library closing at six.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Tushar have at the march?
qa.a: Tushar felt fear, heart hammering when the police looked over, and also pride and closeness when everyone sang together.

qa.q: What made Tushar's decision to join a careful one?
qa.a: Tushar weighed the lab record and family worry, joined a peaceful march with a friend, and left at the planned time.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt holding the other end of the banner?
qa.a: Usha probably felt glad and supported, since the message left the choice free and Tushar still chose to come.

grounding: Tushar's diary shows a young adult joining a peaceful protest, feeling fear, pride and solidarity while weighing studies and family.
